newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Shipowner Tung named Hong Kong leader-in-waiting.
newsitem.headline: Shipowner Tung named Hong Kong leader-in-waiting.

text.p: Hong Kong passed a major milestone in its transition to Chinese rule on Wednesday when billionaire shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa swept to a landslide victory in the race to become governor-elect.

Hong Kong's new political elite, members of a 400-strong electoral college carefully assembled by Beijing, gathered in a hall under a spotlit red and gold seal of the Communist Party of China to hand Tung the post of chief executive-designate.

The outcome was widely regarded in Hong Kong as a foregone conclusion. Tung, whose family maritime empire was bailed out by Beijing a decade ago, had been regarded as China's man since he was singled out for a pointed handshake by China's President Jiang Zemin in January.
Newspapers put the finishing touches to their front pages a day earlier ready to hit the streets the moment the 59-year-old businessman was declared leader-in-waiting.

Tung polled 80 percent of the votes cast by the panel, many of whom are expected to seek influential positions in the post-1997 administration, eclipsing his two rivals, former chief justice Yang Ti Liang and businessman Peter Woo.

Tung, whose wealthy family fled the 1949 communist revolution, will take the helm at midnight on June 30, 1997, stepping into Governor Chris Patten's shoes when the British wind up more than 150 years of colonial rule and Hong Kong once again becomes a part of China.
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen declared the vote the birth of true democracy in Hong Kong, with all 28 governors having been appointed by Britain in the past.
Outside, noisy pro-democracy activists denounced the process as a travesty and set fire to a replica of a traditional Chinese tomb symbolising what they said was the death of democracy.
Police arrested 29 protesters for obstruction, including one of Hong Kong's best-known independent politicians, Emily Lau, who was dragged away kicking and screaming.
Tung, accompanied by bodyguards for the first time, declared his victory a triumph not just for himself but for the entire Chinese nation.

"For the past 100 years, Hong Kong has been a colony. Now we are in charge of ourselves. I believe most Hong Kong people have confidence in the future," he said in a victory speech which stressed the need for stability and played down democracy.

Hong Kong's democrats, who have spearheaded the campaign for greater democracy in Hong Kong, view Tung's conservatism with trepidation and fear his business dealings mean he will be unable to stand up to Beijing.
"The people of Hong Kong cannot trust him to protect our rights...I cannot see how he is in a position to say no to Beijing on any important issue," said legislator Martin Lee.

While some fret over his conservatism, those who know him both at home and abroad hail Tung's good character, his modesty, wisdom and caution -- all qualities he will need to draw on in what promises to be a politically-charged countdown to 1997.
In contrast to the concerns expressed by Hong Hong's politicians, the business community took comfort in the prospect of seeing one of their own at the helm after the handover.
Hong Kong's blue chip Hang Seng index rallied on the news, although it later dropped on interest rate concerns.
China was the first to congratulate Hong Kong's future chief executive. "We would like to congratulate Mr Tung," Qian, making his second trip to Hong Kong for the occasion, told the electoral panel.
British Prime Minister John Major and Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind both sent messages of congratulation to Tung and said he was most welcome to visit Britain whenever he wanted.
Taipei said it hoped to forge cordial ties with Tung.
Patten congratulated his successor and pledged assistance in the months ahead as Tung begins to assemble his administration.

"Governing Hong Kong is not a straightforward or easy job. Only Tung Chee-hwa and I will know over the coming years just how tough it can be," said Patten, who angered China by introducing democratic reforms ahead of the handover.

One of Tung's first tasks is to supervise the appointment of a controversial provisional interim legislature to replace the elected chamber. China's decision to dissolve the chamber was its response to the reforms sponsored by Patten.
Tung crossed the border into China late on Wednesday to attend a meeting on Thursday at which he was expected to receive China's official blessing as Hong Kong's chief executive-designate.
